Sunlight looks white, but it’s actually a mixture of many colors, from red and orange to blue and violet. You can see these colors when a prism splits sunlight into a rainbow.

Light travels in waves, and different colors have different wavelengths. Blue light has shorter waves than red light.

As sunlight enters Earth’s atmosphere, it bumps into tiny molecules of gases such as nitrogen and oxygen. These molecules scatter light in all directions. But they scatter short-wavelength blue light much more strongly than long-wavelength red light. So, wherever you look in the sky, lots of scattered blue light reaches your eyes.

This effect is called **Rayleigh scattering**.

You might wonder: if violet light has an even shorter wavelength, why isn’t the sky violet? Sunlight contains less violet light, our eyes are less sensitive to it, and some violet is absorbed high in the atmosphere. Together, these effects make the sky look blue.

At sunrise and sunset, sunlight travels through more atmosphere before reaching you. Much of the blue light is scattered away along the way, leaving more red and orange light to reach your eyes.

In space, there’s almost no atmosphere to scatter sunlight, so the sky looks black—even when the Sun is shining.

The sky looks blue because of the way sunlight interacts with the air around Earth.

When you look up, some of that scattered blue light reaches your eyes from all directions. That is why the sky looks blue even when you are not looking toward the Sun.

A **browser cache** is a temporary storage area where your browser keeps copies of files from websites you visit. These can include images, fonts, stylesheets, scripts, and sometimes entire pages.

Imagine visiting a news website. The first time, your browser downloads the site’s logo and other files from the website’s server. It may save some of those files in its cache. When you visit again, the browser can reuse the saved copies instead of downloading everything again.

This makes pages load faster, reduces data usage, and puts less demand on the website’s server.

Websites send instructions that help the browser decide **what can be cached and for how long**. Once a cached copy is considered old, the browser may ask the server whether it has changed. If it hasn’t, the browser can keep using the saved copy; if it has, the browser downloads the newer version.

Sometimes a cached file can cause a page to look outdated or behave unexpectedly. Refreshing the page may help, and clearing the cache forces the browser to download fresh copies. However, the next visit may be slower because the browser has to rebuild its cache.

A cache isn’t a complete offline copy of the web: many pages still need an internet connection.

One year into engineering management, I’ve learned that the job isn’t about having all the answers. It’s about creating the conditions for a team to find them together.

A few lessons I’m taking into year two:

• **Listen before solving.** Sometimes people need a sounding board, not a solution.

• **Clarity is kindness.** Clear priorities, expectations, and feedback make work better for everyone.

• **Your calendar reflects your priorities.** If coaching and team health matter, make time for them.

• **Delegation is a form of trust.** Giving people ownership means giving them room to make decisions—and learn.

• **Technical work still matters.** You may write less code, but you need enough context to ask good questions and support sound decisions.

• **Celebrate progress.** It’s easy to move straight to the next problem. Pause to recognize the people who got you this far.

I’m grateful to the teammates and mentors who made the first year a learning experience.

What’s one lesson you learned early in management?

My first year as an engineering manager taught me that the job is less about having the answers and more about creating the conditions for others to do their best work.

A few lessons I am taking into year two:

1. Listening is work. The most valuable part of a one on one is often the question I ask, not the advice I give.

2. Clarity is kindness. Clear priorities and honest feedback prevent confusion from becoming frustration.

3. Delegation is not abandonment. Agree on the outcome, provide context, and stay available without taking the work back.

4. Team health is an engineering concern. Sustainable pace, trust, and psychological safety affect what we build and how well we build it.

5. You will not get everything right. Own mistakes, ask for feedback, and adjust.

I am grateful to the teammates who challenged me and helped me grow. What lesson shaped your first year as a manager?

**Pride and Prejudice** by Jane Austen follows Elizabeth Bennet, one of five sisters in a family whose estate will pass to a male relative when their father dies. Because the sisters have limited financial prospects, their mother is eager to see them married.

Elizabeth meets the wealthy Mr. Darcy, whose apparent arrogance and dismissive behavior lead her to dislike him. Her prejudice deepens when the charming officer George Wickham tells her that Darcy has treated him unjustly. Meanwhile, Elizabeth’s sister Jane falls in love with Darcy’s friend Mr. Bingley, but the couple is separated, partly through Darcy’s intervention.

When Darcy proposes to Elizabeth, she rejects him, accusing him of pride and cruelty. He then explains his actions in a letter, revealing Wickham’s dishonesty. As Elizabeth revises her judgments, Darcy also changes, becoming more considerate and helping rescue her family from scandal after Wickham elopes with her youngest sister. Elizabeth and Darcy eventually recognize their love and marry, while Jane reunites with Bingley.

The novel explores how pride and prejudice distort perception, and how self-knowledge makes personal growth possible. It also examines the pressures of class, wealth, and marriage in a society where women’s security often depends on finding a husband.

**Pride and Prejudice by Jane Austen**

Elizabeth Bennet is one of five sisters whose future security depends largely on marriage. When the wealthy Mr. Bingley rents a nearby estate, he falls in love with Elizabeth’s gentle elder sister, Jane. His friend Mr. Darcy, however, seems arrogant and dismissive, particularly toward Elizabeth.

Elizabeth’s dislike of Darcy deepens when the charming officer Mr. Wickham claims that Darcy treated him unfairly. Darcy later proposes to Elizabeth, but she rejects him, accusing him of arrogance and of separating Jane from Bingley. In a letter, Darcy explains his actions and reveals that Wickham is dishonest.

As Elizabeth reconsiders her judgments, she discovers Darcy’s generosity and loyalty. When her younger sister Lydia elopes with Wickham, Darcy quietly intervenes to arrange their marriage, protecting the Bennet family from scandal. Bingley returns and proposes to Jane. Darcy and Elizabeth eventually acknowledge their changed feelings and become engaged.

The novel explores how pride and prejudice distort perception, while showing that self-knowledge can make love possible. It also examines the pressure on women to marry for financial security and exposes the absurdities of a society governed by wealth, rank, and reputation. Austen treats these serious concerns with wit, irony, and affection for her flawed characters.

**1/5** Simple code beats clever code because code is read far more often than it’s written. Saving five minutes today isn’t worth costing every future reader an hour.

**2/5** Clever code makes the reader ask, “How does this work?” Simple code lets them ask the better question: “Does this solve the problem?”

**3/5** Simple code is easier to debug. When something breaks, clear names, straightforward control flow, and small functions help you find the cause without reverse-engineering a puzzle.

**4/5** Simple doesn’t mean simplistic. Some problems are genuinely complex. The goal is to make that complexity visible and manageable—not hide it behind tricks.

**5/5** Write code for the next person who has to change it. That person might be you, six months from now. If they can understand it quickly, that’s clever enough.

1/ Clever code can be satisfying to write. Simple code is easier to read, change, and trust. Most code is read far more often than it is written.

2/ Simple code makes intent visible. Clear names, small functions, and straightforward control flow help the next reader understand what happens without mentally executing every line.

3/ When something breaks, simple code narrows the search. Fewer hidden assumptions and surprising shortcuts mean fewer places for bugs to hide.

4/ Simple does not mean simplistic. A sophisticated algorithm may be necessary, but its implementation can still use clear names, explicit steps, and comments that explain why.

5/ Cleverness has its place. Use it when it solves a real problem, and measure the benefit. Otherwise, choose the version your teammate can understand on a tired Tuesday afternoon.
